name: What is systemd?
description:
Introduction to systemd

systemd is the init system used by most modern Linux distributions including CentOS 7+, Ubuntu 16+, and Fedora. It manages services (daemons), handles system startup, and much more.

The primary command to interact with systemd is systemctl.

To check if your system uses systemd, run:

$ systemctl --version

You should see output showing the systemd version number.

Let's also check the system state:

$ systemctl is-system-running

If everything is fine, it should say running.

name: Listing Services
description:
Listing Services

To see all active services on the system:

$ systemctl list-units --type=service

This shows a table with columns: UNIT, LOAD, ACTIVE, SUB, and DESCRIPTION.

To see all services (including inactive ones):

$ systemctl list-units --type=service --all

To list only running services:

$ systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running

How many services are currently running on your system?

name: Start, Stop, and Restart
description:
Managing Services

The three most common operations on a service:

Start a service:

$ systemctl start httpd

Stop a service:

$ systemctl stop httpd

Restart a service (stop then start):

$ systemctl restart httpd

Reload configuration without fully restarting:

$ systemctl reload httpd

Try starting the httpd (Apache) service and verify it's running:

$ systemctl start httpd
$ systemctl is-active httpd

It should say active.

name: Checking Service Status
description:
Service Status

To get detailed information about a service:

$ systemctl status httpd

This shows:

  • Whether the service is active (running) or inactive (dead)
  • The process ID (PID)
  • Memory usage
  • Recent log entries

The output includes a tree of processes spawned by the service.

To check just the active state without full details:

$ systemctl is-active httpd

To check if a service failed:

$ systemctl is-failed httpd

name: Enable and Disable at Boot
description:
Boot Behavior

Starting a service only runs it now. To make it start automatically on boot:

$ systemctl enable httpd

This creates a symlink in the systemd boot targets. To verify:

$ systemctl is-enabled httpd

It should say enabled.

To prevent a service from starting at boot:

$ systemctl disable httpd

You can also enable AND start in one command:

$ systemctl enable --now httpd

And disable AND stop:

$ systemctl disable --now httpd
answer: The enable/disable commands only affect boot behavior. They do NOT start or stop the service immediately unless you use --now.

name: Viewing Logs with journalctl
description:
Service Logs

systemd has its own logging system called the journal. Use journalctl to read logs.

View all logs:

$ journalctl

View logs for a specific service:

$ journalctl -u httpd

View only the last 20 lines:

$ journalctl -u httpd -n 20

Follow logs in real-time (like tail -f):

$ journalctl -u httpd -f

Press Ctrl+C to stop following.

View logs since the last boot:

$ journalctl -b

name: Targets (Runlevels)
description:
systemd Targets

In older Linux, we had runlevels (0-6). systemd uses targets instead:

Old Runlevelsystemd TargetPurpose
3multi-user.targetText mode, networking
5graphical.targetGUI desktop
1rescue.targetSingle user / rescue

Check current target:

$ systemctl get-default

Change default target:

$ systemctl set-default multi-user.target

Switch to a target immediately:

$ systemctl isolate rescue.target
answer: Be careful with isolate — it stops all services not required by the target. Don't isolate rescue.target on a remote server or you'll lose SSH!

name: Masking Services
description:
Masking

Sometimes you want to completely prevent a service from being started, even manually. That's what masking does:

$ systemctl mask httpd

Now try to start it:

$ systemctl start httpd

You'll get an error: Failed to start httpd.service: Unit httpd.service is masked.

Masking creates a symlink to /dev/null. To undo:

$ systemctl unmask httpd

Masking is stronger than disable — a disabled service can still be started manually, but a masked service cannot.

This is useful for services that conflict with each other (like iptables vs firewalld).
